items.title: HOMEMADE FIG JAM 🍯 The Secret Ingredient? FIG LEAVES! 🍃
items.description: Today we're making a homemade fig jam, but with a special ingredient: fig leaves! 🍃 This time, we won't use traditional lemon zest to flavor the figs. The goal is to capture that typical summery scent of figs you get when you pass by a fig tree in the summer. And I think the result is truly spectacular! 🍯 INGREDIENTS: 1.5 kg fresh figs 300 g sugar 5 fig leaves Juice of ½ lemon or ½ glass water or wine Once ready, the jam is transferred while still hot into jars and left to cool. 🍃 WHY USE FIG LEAVES? Fig leaves, especially during the summer, release a very distinctive scent. In this recipe, we use them to impart that flavor to the jam, without leaving the leaves inside the jars. The result is a fragrant, sweet fig jam, perfect for breakfast, spread on bread, or paired with a good cheese. 💬 Have you ever used fig leaves in the kitchen? items.title: iGulu LAGER KIT 🍺 Is It Really a Lager? | Tasting & Review
items.description: Today we're testing a homebrewing kit; I'll be trying the iGulu LAGER. 🍺 🍺 iGulu Fermenter / Beer Dispenser $100 Discount Code: CUOREDICIOCCOLATO Link: https://igulu.com/cuoredicioccolato This experiment is particularly interesting because, after using the kit, I also want to recover the yeast that has settled at the bottom and use it for my future Italian Pils, an Italian-style lager that you'll find in our book on homebrewing: https://amzn.to/4sZDU24 The kit contains liquid malt syrup, along with the other ingredients needed for fermentation. Once everything was placed in the fermenter, I started the automatic program. The program included: 10 days of fermentation at 18°C Subsequently lowering the temperature to 4°C for 4 days Tasting after about 14 days And this is precisely where my doubt arises: for a lager, 18°C ​​as a starting temperature seems rather high. For this reason, I've decided that when I brew my all-grain Italian Pils, I'll use MasterCard to manually program the machine and try starting with a fermentation temperature around 12–14°C. As always on the channel, I'll tell you what I really think: I'm not entirely convinced by the kit's program, but in the end, tasting will tell us whether the result is spectacular or not! 😄 🍻 THE TASTING For this tasting, we also have a special guest: Paolo! This time, it won't be just my opinion, because Paolo will help us evaluate the beer and better describe its characteristics. The beer has a beautiful color and is pleasant and fresh. The carbonation, however, isn't particularly high, and the head tends to form quite a bit. And to finish, we served it with a canapé with homemade truffled lard. 🍺🥓 The next experiment will be even more interesting: we'll see if using MasterCard to manually program fermentation can produce a lager closer to the result we're looking for. 📚 HOMEMADE BEER If you're interested in the world of homebrewing, you can find our recipes and experiments in our book, including the Italian Pils, which we'll be making using the yeast recovered from this fermentation. 💬 Have you ever tried a lager kit? items.title: Homemade Mint Liqueur 🌿 Easy Recipe
items.description: Today we're making a delicious homemade mint liqueur! This refreshing liqueur is incredibly easy to prepare using fresh mint leaves, pure alcohol, sugar, water, and a small piece of lemon peel. After just three days of infusion, we'll prepare a simple syrup, combine everything together, and let the liqueur mature for a couple of weeks. The result is a smooth, refreshing mint liqueur with an alcohol content of approximately 42% ABV, perfect served ice cold after dinner or on a hot summer day. This recipe is not included in our first Homemade Liqueurs book because we're saving it for a possible Volume 2. If you'd like to see a second book with even more homemade liqueur recipes, let us know in the comments! Ingredients About 100 fresh mint leaves 250 ml (8.5 fl oz) 96% neutral alcohol (food-grade ethanol) 250 ml (8.5 fl oz) water 100 g (½ cup) sugar A small piece of lemon peel Directions • Infuse the mint leaves and lemon peel in the alcohol for 3 days. • Shake the jar whenever you walk past it. • Prepare a simple syrup using the water and sugar. • Filter the alcohol infusion and mix it with the cooled syrup. • Let the liqueur mature for at least two weeks before tasting. If you make homemade liqueurs and want to calculate the alcohol percentage of your own recipes, visit our website where we've created a free alcohol calculator.
